_about: Known scam formats, distilled from real scam scripts circulating in scammer groups. Contains NO personal data: no names, numbers, emails, addresses or verbatim scripts. Signals are short, generic phrases used to recognise each pattern.

patterns.name: Romance scam: grooming stage
patterns.description: Builds a fast emotional bond before any money is mentioned. Messages are copy-pasted from long templates of love letters, poems and 'good morning' texts.
signals: very intense love declarations within days
calls you 'my husband' or 'my wife' before ever meeting
you are my first and only friend on this site
long lists of personal questions (birthday, favourite colour, ideal partner, gifts you love)
repeated claims of being honest, God-fearing and 'not after your money'
distance, age and language are no barrier to true love
asks to move from the dating site to email, Kik, QQ, Telegram or WhatsApp
generic poems or good-morning messages that read like they were copied
patterns.what_next: Once you feel attached, a crisis appears and they ask for money. The questions you answered can also be used to guess your passwords or security answers.
advice: Insist on a live video call before trusting them
Reverse image search their photos
Never send money, gift cards or crypto to someone you haven't met in person

patterns.name: Romance scam: fake persona
patterns.description: The scammer uses a ready-made life story that explains why they can't meet, call on video, or access their own money.
signals: works offshore on an oil rig or ship
soldier deployed abroad; says details are a 'military secret'
widowed single parent whose spouse died of cancer, with one young child
orphan with no family left
stranded abroad (often West Africa) and staying at a church or mission house
says they can't make video or voice calls for 'security reasons'
has a high salary but no access to their bank account until they return
profile photo isn't theirs ('the account belonged to a colleague')
uses a translator to talk to you
life story contradicts itself (e.g. raised in an orphanage, later raised by mum)
patterns.what_next: The persona is designed so a money request later seems reasonable: they 'can't access' their own money and you are 'the only one' they trust.
advice: Ask detailed questions and watch for contradictions
Real soldiers and oil workers can video call and access their pay
Talk to a friend or family member about the relationship

patterns.name: Romance scam: money request ('billing')
patterns.description: A sudden emergency or opportunity that needs your money urgently. Scammers keep a menu of ready-made stories and rotate them.
signals: child or partner suddenly in hospital; doctor needs a deposit before treatment
a 'doctor' or 'nurse' contacts you saying your partner was injured
school fees for their child, who 'already calls you daddy/mummy'
needs money for a phone so you can finally video call
stuck at a store, short of money, embarrassed
their business is failing; promises to pay back
balance needed for a flight ticket to come and meet you
leave or vacation fee for a deployed soldier
customs, delivery or clearance fee for a package or gift
a big inheritance or 'antiques' deal that will make you both rich
extreme emotional pressure, including threats of self-harm
patterns.what_next: Paying once leads to more requests: hospital bills grow, new fees appear, and the trip never happens.
advice: Do not send money. A real partner will understand
Ask the 'hospital' or 'school' for an official contact you can verify independently
Report the profile to the dating site and your national fraud reporting service

patterns.name: Bank details harvest / money mule
patterns.description: Asks for your card or bank details so a 'lawyer' or 'company' can send money to your account, then asks you to forward part of it. This steals your identity and can make you an accomplice in money laundering.
signals: a lawyer or company will wire money into your account in instalments
asks for full card number, expiry date, card limit or routing number
asks for your SSN, national ID or BVN
asks for your mother's maiden name or other security answers
tells you to withdraw the money and send part via Western Union or crypto
offers you a cut ('keep $500 for yourself')
urgent deadline to provide the details
patterns.what_next: Your account may be emptied or used to move stolen money. When the bank reverses the transfers, you can be held responsible.
advice: Never share card numbers, PINs, ID numbers or security answers
Never receive money for someone and forward it
If you already shared details, call your bank immediately and freeze the card

patterns.name: Sugar daddy / allowance scam
patterns.description: Offers a generous weekly allowance with 'no strings', then asks you to buy a gift card or pay a fee to 'prove your loyalty' before he pays.
signals: offers a weekly allowance to pay your bills
sets 'rules': loyalty, respect, don't talk to other sugar daddies
can't use normal payment apps (account restricted, divorce, hacked)
asks you to buy and activate a gift card to 'test your sincerity'
promises to load a much larger amount onto your card
tells you not to tell anyone about the card
talks about bitcoin mining or trading
patterns.what_next: Once you share the gift card code, the money is gone. Next come 'activation' or 'clearance' fees.
advice: Anyone asking for gift cards is a scammer
Never share gift card numbers or photos of them
Nobody pays you by first making you pay them

patterns.name: Escort / hookup advance payment scam
patterns.description: Promises a paid meeting but demands payment upfront in gift cards and a photo of the scratched card, then disappears or invents more fees.
signals: payment required before meeting
only accepts gift cards (Google Play, Apple, Steam, Amazon)
asks you to scratch the card and send a photo of the code
excuses such as 'I was robbed before, so no cash'
pressure: 'are you ready now?', 'I'm getting dressed to come'
patterns.what_next: The person never shows up. Often a second 'security' or 'driver' fee is requested, sometimes followed by threats.
advice: A photo of a scratched gift card is the same as handing over cash
Stop replying and block the number
Do not pay 'security' or 'driver' fees

patterns.name: Mass dating-site opener ('site bombing')
patterns.description: The same generic opener sent to many profiles to move victims off the platform quickly.
signals: I'm new on this site and my pictures aren't uploaded yet
your profile says we have so much in common (without specifics)
immediately shares an email or messenger ID
very long self-description with body measurements and hobbies
patterns.what_next: Moving off the site removes the platform's protections and reporting tools before the grooming begins.
advice: Keep conversations on the dating platform at first
Be wary of profiles without photos or with very generic messages

patterns.name: AI voice clone family emergency
patterns.description: A call or voice note that sounds exactly like a relative (often a child or grandchild) in an accident, arrested or stranded, demanding urgent money. The voice can be cloned from a few seconds of social media video.
signals: sounds like a family member but calls from a new or unknown number
accident, arrest, hospital or kidnapping emergency
urgent payment by transfer, crypto or gift card
asks you to keep it secret from other family members
a 'lawyer', 'officer' or 'doctor' takes over the call
pressure not to hang up or call anyone back
patterns.what_next: Once you pay, a second 'bail', 'hospital' or 'court' fee follows.
advice: Hang up and call your relative back on the number you already have
Agree on a family code word for real emergencies
Judge the request, not the voice: voices can be faked perfectly

patterns.name: Deepfake boss / executive payment request
patterns.description: An email, message or even a live video call that appears to come from a boss or company executive, asking an employee to make an urgent, confidential payment or change supplier bank details.
signals: urgent, confidential payment request from a 'CEO' or 'director'
new or changed bank details for a supplier or invoice
instructions to bypass normal approval steps
video call where faces or voices seem slightly off, or cameras are 'broken'
sent from a personal email or new phone number
patterns.what_next: The money goes to a scammer-controlled account and is moved on within minutes.
advice: Verify any payment request through a separate, known channel
Never change bank details based on an email or message alone
Follow your company's approval process, even under pressure

patterns.name: Fake investment platform ('pig butchering')
patterns.description: A friendly or romantic contact, built up over weeks or months, introduces you to a 'secret' crypto or trading platform. The app shows huge fake profits to make you invest more.
signals: online friend or partner who talks about their trading or crypto success
asks you to join a specific app or website to invest
guaranteed or very high returns
small first withdrawal works, to win your trust
pressure to invest more before a 'window' closes
withdrawal blocked until you pay 'tax', 'fees' or 'unlock deposit'
patterns.what_next: You can't withdraw. Every withdrawal attempt brings a new fee until you stop paying; then the contact disappears.
advice: Never invest through a platform someone you met online recommends
Check if the platform is registered with your country's financial regulator
If you can't withdraw, stop paying any fees

patterns.name: Recovery scam (scammed twice)
patterns.description: After someone loses money to a scam, a 'lawyer', 'hacker', 'crypto recovery expert' or fake police officer offers to get the money back for an upfront fee.
signals: contacts you after you lost money to a scam
claims to be law enforcement, a lawyer or a recovery service
guarantees to recover your funds
asks for an upfront fee, 'tax' or 'processing' payment
knows details of your earlier loss
patterns.what_next: The fee is stolen too, and more 'fees' follow.
advice: Real police and regulators never charge to recover money
Report losses only through official channels you look up yourself
Warn family members who were scammed before: they are prime targets

patterns.name: Fake bank 'safe account' transfer
patterns.description: A call or message from the 'bank fraud team' says your account is compromised and pressures you to move your money to a 'safe account' or wallet. Because you authorize the transfer yourself, the bank may not refund it.
signals: caller ID or SMS shows your bank's real name or number
says your account has been hacked or flagged
tells you to move money to a 'safe' or 'new' account
asks you to install an app or share your screen
stays on the line while you make the transfer
knows your name and some account details
patterns.what_next: The 'safe account' belongs to the scammer and the money is moved on instantly.
advice: A real bank will never ask you to move money to a 'safe account'
Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
Never install apps or share your screen on a caller's instructions

patterns.name: 'I sent you money by mistake' refund
patterns.description: Money lands in your account or payment app from a stranger, followed by a message begging you to refund it. The original payment is stolen or fake and gets reversed, so your refund is your own money.
signals: unexpected payment from someone you don't know
urgent message: 'I sent it to you by mistake, please send it back'
asks you to refund to a different account or number
fake credit alert or screenshot instead of a real deposit
patterns.what_next: The original payment is reversed or was never real, and you lose what you sent.
advice: Don't refund it yourself: contact your bank or payment app
Check your actual balance in the official app, not a screenshot or SMS
Let the bank handle the reversal

patterns.name: QR code phishing ('quishing')
patterns.description: A fake QR code, often a sticker pasted over a real one on a parking meter, menu, poster or letter, leads to a cloned payment or login page.
signals: QR code sticker placed on top of another one
QR code in an unexpected email, letter or parcel note
the page asks for card details or a login right after scanning
web address doesn't match the business you're paying
patterns.what_next: Card numbers and login details entered on the fake page are stolen and used immediately.
advice: Check the web address after scanning before entering anything
Pay through the official app or website you look up yourself
Report tampered QR codes to the business

patterns.name: Harmful app disguised as a document
patterns.description: A file sent as an invitation, invoice, traffic fine, bank statement or photo that is actually an app (.apk) or program.
signals: file named like an invitation, invoice, fine or statement
ends in .apk or has a double ending like .pdf.apk
asks you to allow 'install from unknown sources'
sent by an unknown number or a hacked friend's account
patterns.what_next: The app can read your SMS codes, steal banking logins and control your phone.
advice: Never install apps sent in chats
Delete the file
If installed, disconnect from the internet and contact your bank

patterns.name: Fake tech or customer support
patterns.description: A pop-up, call, email or message claims your computer, phone or account is hacked or infected, or that you were wrongly charged for a subscription. They push you to call a number, install remote-access software, or pay to 'fix' it.
signals: pop-up or message saying your device is infected or hacked
call this number immediately
install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or another remote-access app
refund for a subscription you didn't order (antivirus, streaming)
asks you to log in to your bank while they watch your screen
asks for payment by gift card, crypto or wire to fix the problem
patterns.what_next: With remote access they can empty your bank account or install harmful software, then often pass you to a fake 'bank' or 'government agent'.
advice: Real companies don't call you about viruses or ask to control your device
Never install remote-access apps for someone who contacted you
Close the pop-up, and contact the company only through its official website

patterns.name: Government or police impersonation
patterns.description: Someone claims to be from the tax office, police, court, immigration or a social security office. They say you owe money, face arrest, or that your ID was used in a crime, and demand urgent payment.
signals: warrant, arrest or deportation threat
unpaid tax, fine or 'case' that must be settled today
payment by gift card, crypto, crypto ATM or wire
told to keep it secret or stay on the line
your national ID or social security number was 'used in a crime'
official-looking badge numbers or documents sent by message
patterns.what_next: After one payment they invent new 'fees'. Some move on to taking your savings 'for safekeeping'.
advice: Government agencies don't demand payment by gift card, crypto or wire
Hang up and contact the agency using a number from its official website
Never pay to avoid an arrest over the phone

patterns.name: Cash to crypto ATM or courier
patterns.description: A scammer tells you to withdraw cash and deposit it into a cryptocurrency ATM, buy gold, or hand cash to a courier, often to 'protect' it or settle a fake debt.
signals: withdraw cash from your bank and deposit it into a Bitcoin ATM
scan this QR code at the crypto ATM
convert your savings to gold or cash for safekeeping
a courier will come to your home to collect it
told to lie to bank staff about why you are withdrawing
patterns.what_next: Money sent through a crypto ATM or handed to a courier is almost impossible to recover.
advice: No real bank, police or government office will ask you to use a crypto ATM or hand over cash or gold
Talk to a trusted family member before withdrawing large sums
If bank staff ask questions, tell them the truth: they are trying to protect you

patterns.name: Investment club with fake celebrity endorsement
patterns.description: An ad or group chat ('investment club', 'VIP signals group') uses AI-made videos of celebrities, business leaders or 'experts' to promote a trading platform or coin.
signals: video of a famous person or CEO promoting a guaranteed investment
invitation to a private WhatsApp or Telegram 'investment club'
'teacher' or 'assistant' gives daily stock or crypto tips
screenshots of other members' huge profits
pressure to move to a specific app to invest
patterns.what_next: Early fake profits encourage bigger deposits, then withdrawals are blocked behind 'fees'.
advice: Celebrities don't promote guaranteed returns in group chats
Check whether the platform is registered with your country's financial regulator
Never invest through an app someone in a chat group recommends

universal_red_flags: payment by gift card, crypto or Western Union
a request to 'prove' trust, loyalty or sincerity with money
urgent emotional crisis plus a deadline
asks for card, bank, ID or security-question details
asks you to receive money and send it on
life story changes or contradicts itself
messages that look copied and pasted
